claims.claim: **Most ingested foreign bodies are low risk** and need no imaging or intervention. ⚠️ **High-risk objects can cause significant harm or death — discuss with a senior clinician or specialist.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Oesophageal button batteries must be removed within two hours.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Surgical review for:** magnets · large objects · anything impacted in the oropharynx. Ingested objects may be toxic — consider Poisons Information (13 11 26).
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Peak incidence 6 months to 3 years**; developmental, behavioural problems and pica raise the risk. **Older children who ingest intentionally need a mental health review.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ask about:** object type and timing · coughing, drooling, painful swallowing, reduced intake, vomiting or abdominal pain, GI bleeding or melaena · **choking or respiratory distress (consider inhalation).**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **High-risk foreign bodies:** oesophageal button battery · a magnet plus metal, or more than 1 magnet · sharp objects in the oesophagus · lead objects that fail to leave the stomach · large objects (over 6 cm long and/or over 2 cm wide) · expandable objects (water beads) · multi-component toys.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Higher impaction risk:** pre-existing GI abnormalities or repaired/unrepaired malformations · eosinophilic oesophagitis · neuromuscular disease.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Examine for** airway compromise, drooling or oropharyngeal injury, respiratory distress, and abdominal tenderness, peritonitis or obstruction.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Image:** suspected or known button battery · magnet(s) or any radio-opaque object that is high risk · object not known · child who is unwell or high-risk. **In smaller children, one X-ray covering neck, chest and abdomen.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Imaging may be skipped only if ALL apply:** asymptomatic · normal examination · no known GI abnormality · reassuring observation · eating and drinking · object under 2 cm diameter and under 6 cm long, **not a magnet or battery**, non-expandable and non-toxic.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Critically unwell children and high-risk objects (button battery, magnets, sharp or lead objects) need time-critical care.** The referral team (ENT, general surgery or gastroenterology) depends on local service, object and site.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Oesophageal button battery: honey for children over 1 year, within 12 hours of ingestion, while awaiting theatre — up to 6 doses of 10 mL, one every 10 minutes.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Batteries in the stomach or beyond without signs of GI injury:** discuss with the relevant specialist for a plan and timeframe.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **A single magnet seen on X-ray can still be high risk** — two stuck together can look like one.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Water beads (superabsorbent polymers)** can pass the pylorus, then expand enough to obstruct the bowel — **discuss early with Poisons Information** about growth potential and endoscopic removal.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Objects impacted in the oropharynx need urgent ENT evaluation**; the tonsils are a place fish bones can lodge.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Oesophageal food bolus:** ⚠️ **acutely symptomatic (drooling, neck or chest pain) → urgent endoscopy**; if managing secretions, discuss early with paediatric gastroenterology for retrieval within 12–24 hours.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Carbonated drinks may help mobilise a food bolus** (may cause vomiting). ⚠️ **Glucagon and hyoscine butylbromide are not recommended in children.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Coins and blunt objects:** symptomatic → urgent endoscopy; **asymptomatic oesophageal object → endoscopic removal within 24 hours**; over 6 cm long → gastroenterology or surgical opinion. **A diameter over 2 cm (Australian 10c, 20c, 50c, $1) is unlikely to pass a young child's pylorus.**
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consult the relevant specialty when:** symptomatic · immediate removal needed · FB lodged in the oesophagus · toxicity concern · significant past history or behavioural issues.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discharge when** the child is well-looking and free of pain, without respiratory distress, eating and drinking, and has a reliable history of a low-risk FB.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Return if:** fever · vomiting · abdominal pain · breathing problems · food and drink not tolerated · melaena or haematemesis.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Foreign body ingestion' (Last updated February 2024), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Foreign_body_ingestion/, retrieved 2026-09-23
